Cubit
KYOO-bit
n.
Latin cubitum, “elbow”; the unit of measurement based on the length of the human forearm from elbow to tip of middle finger. Hebrew ’ammāh, Greek pēchus. Standardized at approximately 18 inches (45 cm); the “long cubit” (Ezek 40:5) was about 21 inches (53 cm).

Biblical Definition

The cubit is the standard ancient unit of linear measurement throughout the Bible—the length from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger of a man, approximately 18 inches (45 cm) for the common cubit and approximately 21 inches (53 cm) for the long cubit used in Ezekiel’s temple vision. The cubit governs the measurements of every significant sacred structure described in Scripture. Noah’s ark: the length of the ark shall be three hundred cubits, the breadth of it fifty cubits, and the height of it thirty cubits (Gen 6:15)—a vessel approximately 450 feet long, 75 feet wide, and 45 feet tall, of sufficient capacity to carry the preserved pairs of animal kinds through the flood. The tabernacle’s detailed measurements (Ex 25-27) are given in cubits: the ark of the covenant was two-and-a-half cubits long, one-and-a-half cubits broad, one-and-a-half cubits high; the table of shewbread was two cubits long, one cubit broad, one-and-a-half cubits high; the brazen altar was five cubits square and three cubits high; the tabernacle court was 100 cubits long and 50 cubits broad. Solomon’s temple measurements (1 Kgs 6) are given in cubits: the house was 60 cubits long, 20 cubits broad, and 30 cubits high; the holy of holies was 20 cubits cubed; the porch was 20 cubits broad and 10 cubits deep. Ezekiel’s prophetic temple vision uses the cubit extensively (Ezek 40-48). And the New Jerusalem of Revelation 21:17 is measured: and he measured the wall thereof, an hundred and forty and four cubits, according to the measure of a man, that is, of the angel. The cubit therefore has a deep structural function in biblical narrative: it provides the unit by which God’s sacred architecture is given concrete dimensions, by which the ark of salvation is sized to its purpose, by which the worship-spaces of God’s people are designed, and by which the eschatological architecture of the New Jerusalem is described. Christ Himself uses the cubit figuratively in the Sermon on the Mount: which of you by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature? If ye then be not able to do that thing which is least, why take ye thought for the rest? (Luke 12:25-26). The smallest addition to one’s own life is beyond the worried soul’s power; how then should anxiety be permitted to govern the larger matters?

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines CUBIT as the forearm; the distance from the elbow to the extremity of the middle finger, which was the original cubit; in the scripture, a measure of 1 1/2 feet (about 18 inches), used for the dimensions of the ark, the tabernacle, the temple, and the New Jerusalem.

expand to see more

CUBIT, n. — 1. In anatomy, the forearm; the ulna, a bone of the arm from the elbow to the wrist. 2. In mensuration, the distance from the elbow to the extremity of the middle finger, which was the original cubit. The Hebrew cubit was equal to 21.888 inches; the Roman cubit was about 17.5 inches; common cubit, 18 inches.

MEASURE, n. — The whole extent or dimensions of any thing; size; quantity; that by which any thing is computed.

Key Scripture

Genesis 6:15 — "And this is the fashion which thou shalt make it of: The length of the ark shall be three hundred cubits, the breadth of it fifty cubits, and the height of it thirty cubits."

Exodus 25:10 — "And they shall make an ark of shittim wood: two cubits and a half shall be the length thereof, and a cubit and a half the breadth thereof, and a cubit and a half the height thereof."

Luke 12:25-26 — "And which of you with taking thought can add to his stature one cubit? If ye then be not able to do that thing which is least, why take ye thought for the rest?"

Revelation 21:17 — "And he measured the wall thereof, an hundred and forty and four cubits, according to the measure of a man, that is, of the angel."

Modern Corruption

The cubit as a biblical unit is corrupted in modern reading chiefly by being treated as a quaint pre-metric historical curiosity rather than as the structural unit by which God’s sacred architecture is concretely designed; recovery requires reading the cubit-measurements with appreciation for the precision and theological substance they carry.

expand to see more

The contemporary reader, faced with the cubit-measurements of Scripture, tends to convert them quickly to modern equivalents and move on. The biblical writers used the cubit with detailed precision, and the precision is theologically substantive. Noah’s ark’s dimensions (300x50x30 cubits) yield a ratio (10:1.67:1) remarkably similar to that of modern oceangoing vessels designed for stability in heavy seas—the ark was not a fanciful boat-of-the-imagination but a vessel of sound naval architecture. The tabernacle’s measurements describe a portable sanctuary of specific proportions that the LORD Himself commanded—each dimension carrying typological significance the rabbis and church fathers explored across the centuries (the holy of holies as cubical, anticipating the New Jerusalem; the proportions of the ark itself; the relation of the parts to the whole). Solomon’s temple’s measurements show the holy of holies as a perfect cube of 20 cubits—and Revelation 21 ends with the New Jerusalem itself being a perfect cube of 12,000 furlongs, the consummate eschatological echo. The cubit-measurements are therefore not numerical filler but the concrete dimensional substance of God’s sacred architecture across redemptive history.

Christ’s figurative use of the cubit in the Sermon on the Mount is sharply pastoral. Which of you by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature? The smallest measurable addition to one’s own being (the cubit being not random but the smallest standardized unit a hearer would clearly visualize) is beyond the worried soul’s power. The argument moves from least to greatest: if the soul cannot add one cubit by anxiety, how then should anxiety be permitted to govern the larger matters of food, clothing, future? The figure depends on the cubit’s being the smallest familiar unit; lose the cubit-vocabulary, and Christ’s argument loses some of its sharpness. Recover the cubit, recover the precision, recover the theological substance the cubit-measurements carry across the canon: the ark of salvation through the flood, the tabernacle and temple of God’s dwelling among His people, the New Jerusalem of the consummate eschatological hope—all concretely measured in the cubit Scripture itself uses.

Hebrew Roots

Latin cubitum (elbow), Hebrew ’ammāh, Greek pēchus—the standard ancient unit of linear measurement based on the human forearm; structural to the dimensions of Noah’s ark, the tabernacle, Solomon’s temple, Ezekiel’s prophetic temple, and the New Jerusalem; used figuratively by Christ for the smallest measurable addition to one’s own being.

expand to see more

Hebrew ’ammāh (H520) — cubit (the standard linear unit; over 240 OT uses).

Greek pēchus (G4083) — cubit (the NT term; Matt 6:27; Luke 12:25; John 21:8; Rev 21:17).

Hebrew long cubit (royal or sacred cubit) — approximately 21 inches (Ezek 40:5).

Hebrew common cubit — approximately 18 inches (the standard everyday unit).
